Semiconductor Workers’ Walkout Disrupts Operations Across Zambia’s Main Chip Plants

LUSAKA—Production at Zambia’s leading semiconductor manufacturing plants came to a halt Tuesday as a wave of worker walkouts continued for a third straight day, leaving assembly lines silent and hundreds of employees gathered outside main gates.

The strike, led by the Zambia Semiconductor Workers’ Union (ZSWU), began early Monday at ChipTech Zambia’s Lusaka fabrication facility. Workers at microchip and component plants operated by NanoCore Manufacturing and Zambezi Silicon Solutions quickly joined, citing disputes over wage increases, working conditions, and overtime compensation.

“We have been negotiating for months, but management has not addressed our concerns about fair pay and safety measures,” said ZSWU General Secretary Linda Mwewa, addressing a crowd of workers outside the ChipTech plant. “Until our voices are heard, we will remain outside.”

Company representatives acknowledged the impact. “We are committed to constructive dialogue with our workforce to resolve these issues as soon as possible,” said a spokesperson for NanoCore Manufacturing. “In the meantime, our Lusaka and Ndola sites have suspended production.”

Industry analysts estimate that more than 1,100 workers across the three companies have joined the walkout, affecting both wafer fabrication and chip assembly lines. According to the Zambia Semiconductor Industry Association, the combined sites account for approximately 80% of the country’s semiconductor output, which includes microprocessors and memory chips used in consumer and industrial products.

“Any significant stoppage in these plants will impact monthly output targets and could lead to delays in fulfilling both domestic and export orders,” said analyst Patrick Mwila of Lusaka Industrial Research Institute. “The longer the dispute lasts, the harder it will be to recover lost production.”

Although company officials have stressed that safety and security teams remain on-site, many workers say their main concern is achieving a sustainable resolution. “We’re ready to return to work, but only if management comes forward with a fair offer,” said Joseph Banda, an assembly technician at Zambezi Silicon Solutions.

Negotiations between union leaders and company officials were set to resume late Tuesday, but as of press time, no agreement had been reached and the walkout continued.
